extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and readers of prose and poetry interested in the nature and evaluation of wit/humour
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging 'wit' (including puns, epigrams, metaphors, anagrams, acrostics, chronograms, doggerel, etc.), as discussed in an 18th-century essay. Emphasises distinctions between true, false, and mixed wit and tests for punning.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit: resemblance of ideas that gives delight and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: True Wit generally consists in such a Resemblance and Congruity of Ideas as gives Delight and Surprise to the Reader; the resemblance must not be too obvious or lying too near in the nature of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's account (quoted) is used to explain wit as 'the Assemblage of Ideas' producing 'pleasant Pictures and agreeable Visions in the Fancy.' Examples: a simile that adds an unexpected second quality (e.g. 'the Bosom of his Mistress is as white as Snow' becomes wit when he adds 'and cold too'). True wit covers metaphors, similitudes, allegories, enigmas, mottos, parables, fables, dramatic burlesque and methods of allusion. Scoring note: judge by degree of surprise and delight produced, and by how far the resemblance rests on idea (truth) rather than mere sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: False wit: resemblance of letters/words/sounds (mechanical devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: False Wit chiefly consists in the Resemblance and Congruity of single Letters (anagrams, chronograms, lipograms, acrosticks), of Syllables (echos, doggerel rhymes), of Words (punns, quibbles), or of whole sentences/poems cast into shapes; it is a resemblance of words rather than ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many examples and anti-patterns are given: Anagrams, Acrosticks, Chronograms, Lipograms, Bouts-Rimés, double rhymes, and shaped poems are treated as 'false' because they rely on letter/word tricks. Chronograms focus on extracting dates/figures rather than thought. Scoring note: these devices may show ingenuity or labor but not necessarily 'wit' — penalise where meaning/substance is sacrificed for mechanical cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixt wit (mixed word-and-idea wit) and its proper province
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixt Wit consists partly in the Resemblance of Ideas and partly in the Resemblance of Words; it mixes true wit and punnish devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay locates mixt wit chiefly in epigram and 'little occasional Poems' (e.g., Cowley); it is 'more or less perfect as the Resemblance lies in the Ideas or in the Words.' Guidance: reserve mixed devices for short forms (epigrams); evaluate by balance: the more the resemblance rests on ideas/truth, the more successful. Anti-pattern: overreliance on wordplay that undermines the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of punning/paranomasia
rubrics_metrics.description: A Punn is a conceit arising from the use of two Words that agree in the Sound, but differ in the Sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punning is ubiquitous and persistent (historical examples given). It is named as a common 'jingle of words' and placed among figures of speech. Evaluate puns by whether they contribute to sense/delight or are mere sound-play; treat gratuitous puns as 'false wit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for distinguishing true wit from a pun
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to try a Piece of Wit (specifically a pun) is to translate it into a different Language: If it bears the Test, you may pronounce it true; if it vanishes in the Experiment, you may conclude it to have been a Punn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit diagnostic: translate the phrase — if the cleverness survives beyond language-specific homophony, it's more likely to be substantive wit. Scoring note: use cross-linguistic resilience as a strong indicator of idea-based wit rather than mere sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential properties of wit: delight and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: For a resemblance of ideas to count as Wit it is necessary that the Ideas give Delight and Surprise to the Reader — especially Surprise is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge pieces by presence of these two properties. Examples: ordinary obvious similes do not produce surprise and therefore are not wit; unexpected secondary qualities added to a simile create wit. Scoring: weight surprise most highly, then delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation of wit in truth and good sense (Bouhours)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Basis of all Wit is Truth; no Thought can be valuable of which good Sense is not the Ground-work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bouhours' precept: beautiful thought must be just and founded in the nature of things. Evaluate by checking whether the clever resemblance rests on a truthful, sensible relation rather than fanciful or forced contrivance. Anti-pattern: artifice without truth (contrived epithets, strained analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of words and thoughts adapted to subject (Dryden) — caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden: 'Wit... is a Propriety of Words and Thoughts adapted to the Subject.' (quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that this definition is very broad — it would stretch to include many forms of good writing beyond wit. Use it as a reminder to assess fit/propriety, but do not conflate general 'good writing' with wit specifically. Scoring note: propriety is necessary but not sufficient for wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between wit and judgment (Locke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit lies in assembling ideas quickly and finding resemblances; Judgment lies in separating carefully to avoid being misled by similitude — they are different faculties and not always coexistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to temper evaluation: a piece may be very witty (quick associations) but lack sound judgment (accuracy or appropriateness). Conversely, judged prose may lack liveliness. When assessing overall quality, consider both faculties: wit for freshness, judgment for correctness and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overvaluing rhyme and doggerel: rhyme cannot rescue poor thought
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Thought of the Couplet in doggerel is good, the Rhyme adds little; and if bad, it will not be in the Power of the Rhyme to recommend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: double rhymes, doggerel admired by ignorant readers — evaluate primarily on the quality of thought and wit, not on rhyme cleverness alone. Anti-pattern: rewarding mere rhythmic or rhyming cleverness when the idea is empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint-games and contrived tasks (Bouts-Rimés, chronograms, acrostics) are inferior when they subordinate thought to form
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices like Bouts-Rimés (lists of rhymes to be filled), chronograms (inscriptions encoding dates), acrosticks, and similar puzzles prize mechanical skill in accommodating external constraints over genuine thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises may show ingenuity or skill with form, but should be judged harshly if they detract from meaning, truth, or surprise. Example: chronograms on medals value the year more than the thought; Bouts-Rimés can be rendered meaningless if the rhymes are forced or common. Scoring note: penalize where constraint dictates content rather than enhances it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigram as the proper vehicle for mixed/epigrammatic wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The only province for mixt Wit is Epigram, or little occasional Poems 'that in their own Nature are nothing else but a Tissue of Epigrams.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve heavily verbal or mixed puns and paradoxes for short, epigrammatic forms. Evaluate longer works on idea coherence and truth; allow denser wordplay in epigrams but judge balance of idea vs word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antithesis and opposition as sources of wit (in addition to resemblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only resemblance, but Opposition of Ideas very often produces Wit (turns, antitheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating wit, look also for clever oppositions and antitheses that create surprise and insight. This broadens the search beyond mere metaphor/similarity to include contrast-based cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual note: prevalence and persistence of punning
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning is a persistent 'Weed' of human speech — seeds of punning exist in everyone's mind, and unless cultivated by rules of art can resurge even in learned ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging contemporary usage, be aware of historical taste: presence of puns is not per se disqualifying, but their prevalence may indicate decline in taste. Use norms of the current audience/genre: puns may be acceptable in certain comedy or convivial contexts but not in serious poetical or critical prose.
